entry.evidence: The forcing of seasonal to interannual SST variability during this and other notable climatic transitions, however, remains unexplored.

steps.action: The authors review published low-resolution SST reconstructions from the western tropical North Atlantic, which disagree: some show a slightly warmer YD, Lea et al. show a cooler YD in Cariaco.
steps.quote: different reconstructions have yielded inconsistent results

steps.action: The authors pose the question of how seasonal to interannual SST variability in the TNA responded to the YD-Holocene transition, which mean-state records cannot resolve.
steps.quote: The forcing of seasonal to interannual SST variability during this and other notable climatic transitions, however, remains unexplored.

steps.action: The authors apply mass spectrometry imaging of alkenones at 100-µm resolution, a technique developed in their earlier work (refs 9, 10, 53, 54), with its sample preparation and quality thresholds.
steps.quote: by means of MSI10 at 100-µm resolution in a 60-cm section of the well-dated core MD03-2621

steps.action: The authors select a 60-cm varved section of core MD03-2621 that spans about 11.9 to 11.2 kyr b2k. It uses the inherited Deplazes et al. age model, tuned to NGRIP, with greyscale matched to reflectance to correct depth offsets.
steps.quote: This section spans an age of approximately 11.9 to 11.2 kyr b2k and thus includes the YD–Holocene transition

steps.action: The authors run MALDI FT-ICR MSI on thin sections, obtaining about 20,000 spots per 5-cm slice with C37:2 and C37:3 alkenone intensities, plus µXRF elemental maps and greyscale images.
steps.quote: Around 20,000 individual spots were thereby obtained for every 5-cm slice

steps.action: The authors pool spots into 1-year horizons (at least ten spots each), convert MSI to GC-equivalent U37K' values and translate them to SST with BAYSPLINE. Annual mean SST is 23.8 °C both before and after the transition.
steps.quote: our high-resolution reconstructions indicate that annually averaged SST remained constant across the YD–Holocene transition

steps.action: The authors extract the sediment slices after MSI and analyse them by GC-FID, giving an MSI-to-GC ratio of 1.194 ± 0.021 and conventional SST values that match the MSI record (Extended Data Fig. 1b).
steps.quote: after MSI, sediment slices were extracted for conventional proxy analysis

steps.action: The authors compare the MSI record with the independent conventional U37K' record of Herbert and Schuffert (ODP 1002), which agrees, and with Lea et al.'s Mg/Ca record, which shows YD cooling.
steps.quote: with those previously reported by Herbert and Schuffert23 but different from the YD cooling described by Lea et al.3

steps.action: The authors propose that the conflicting low-resolution records are explained by seasonal effects and changes in water-column stratification, not by a change in annual mean SST.
steps.quote: conflicting, low-resolution SST records from the Cariaco Basin and the TNA can be explained by seasonal effects and changes to water-column stratification

steps.action: The authors observe three SST maxima at about 11.50 to 11.45 kyr b2k, coinciding with the Preboreal oscillation, about 1.3 °C above the adjacent 50 years.
steps.quote: Three prominent SST maxima are observed between about 11.50 to 11.45 kyr b2k

steps.action: The authors age-correct Lea et al.'s foraminiferal record and find two warm points at 11.43 and 11.50 kyr b2k, plus a coincident light-sediment (upwelling) excursion, both consistent with the PBO maxima (Extended Data Fig. 2).
steps.quote: A warm tropical response to the PBO would be supported by the lower-resolution foraminiferal SST record of Lea et al.3

steps.action: The authors run REDFIT spectral, Morlet wavelet and 2-8-year band-pass analyses. These show 120- and 42-year cycles and a significant strengthening of sub-decadal variability at 11.66 kyr b2k (t-test).
steps.quote: The variability at sub-decadal frequencies is weak during the late YD but substantially strengthens at 11.66 kyr b2k (P = 0.006)

steps.action: The authors revisit the sprayed-extract precision experiment to model analytical variability against spot number. They subtract it from observed variability to remove the artefact of fewer spots per thinner Holocene varve; the increase persists.
steps.quote: the trend towards higher interannual variability in the Holocene persists (Fig. 2c)

steps.action: The authors check the premise of an ENSO teleconnection to Cariaco SST with the modern MEI.v2 index and HadISST anomalies, 1980-2020.
steps.quote: From the nine positive ENSO events detected, eight (six) resulted in positive spring (annual) SST anomalies.

steps.action: The authors set the muted late-YD interannual variability against model hypotheses of stronger ENSO under AMOC collapse and against foraminifera-based mid-YD ENSO estimates. They note their record covers only the last two YD centuries.
steps.quote: The muted interannual SST variability during the late YD thus seems to stand in conflict with the hypothesis

steps.action: Drawing on Cheng et al., the authors propose a muted ENSO teleconnection during the late YD. They attribute the Holocene strengthening to the northward ITCZ shift or to sea-ice retreat.
steps.quote: A muted ENSO teleconnection during the late YD would thus be feasible

steps.action: The authors check that laminae are annual couplets using µXRF on spots congruent with MSI: dark layers are rich in Fe, Ti and Ca (non-upwelling) and light layers in Si (upwelling). They also check that alkenones are deposited year-round (Extended Data Figs 5, 6; §5.10).
steps.quote: we confirmed that the investigated laminae couplets represent annual cycles, as already proposed by Hughen et al.18

steps.action: The authors assign single-spot U37K' values to seasons by a greyscale threshold, compute 5-year seasonality and fit ramps (RAMPFIT, Mann-Whitney test). Seasonality rises abruptly from 0.8 to 1.8 °C at 11.64 kyr b2k.
steps.quote: SST seasonality substantially strengthened into the Holocene (P < 0.001)

steps.action: The authors vary the greyscale threshold over a range of ΔGS (Extended Data Fig. 8) and fit both unconstrained and constrained ramps; the seasonality increase holds in all cases.
steps.quote: [...] is robust across a range of sediment colour values chosen to separate data into upwelling and non-upwelling seasons

steps.action: The authors compare reconstructed early Holocene seasonality with modern Cariaco seasonality from HadISST for 1980-2020 (1.6 °C).
steps.quote: Reconstructed early Holocene seasonality is thus similar to the modern Cariaco Basin (1.6 °C).

steps.action: The authors attribute the seasonality increase to a northward shift and/or wider annual range of the ITCZ, reinforced by local stratification and peak insolation seasonality (Extended Data Fig. 9a).
steps.quote: we posit that both were forced by the position of the ITCZ

steps.action: The authors propose that Lea et al.'s abrupt Mg/Ca warming records the warmer, stratified non-upwelling season, because G. ruber prefers that season (sediment-trap fluxes, Extended Data Fig. 9b).
steps.quote: The abrupt warming inferred by Lea et al.3 might actually reflect increased SST in the thermally stratified water column of the non-upwelling season

steps.action: The authors convert the seasonal SST difference into an annual amplitude, assuming a sinusoid, to compute the warm-season warming a G. ruber record would show.
steps.quote: can be converted into annual SST amplitude by assuming a sinusoidal curve

steps.action: The authors compare the computed 1.5-1.9 °C increase in seasonal amplitude with the warming in Lea et al.'s record and find them similar.
steps.quote: which is similar to the warming described by Lea et al.3

steps.action: The authors keep the conclusions that annual mean SST was stable while seasonal and interannual variability increased, and that high-frequency SST variability is sensitive to changes in climate background.
steps.quote: we conclude that the high-frequency component of the climate system can be especially sensitive to changes in climate background

end.claim: Across the YD-Holocene transition in the Cariaco Basin, annual mean SST stayed stable while SST seasonality increased more than twofold to near-modern 1.6 °C and interannual variability intensified.

decisive_move.sentence: Assigning single-spot MSI alkenone data to upwelling and non-upwelling seasons by sediment colour is what yields the seasonality estimate; without it the headline claim of a twofold seasonality increase would not exist.

gates.evidence: Data acquisition was motivated by an open question (§1 ¶3), not by a stated hypothesis; the ITCZ and ENSO explanations come after the data (§3 ¶2, §4 ¶2). The seasonality and variability increases faced tests they could have failed: significance tests (P = 0.006, P < 0.001), an analytical-variability correction (§5.9 ¶2) and a threshold sweep (Extended Data Fig. 8). The ITCZ mechanism faced no such test. Thresholds were chosen by maximizing the seasonal difference after seeing the data (§5.7 ¶1); nothing was preregistered.

limits: No peer review file was supplied, although the paper states that reports are available, so no review sequence is coded. Sub-claims and their statuses: the ITCZ position/range forcing of seasonality is best_explanation (posited, not tested against a rival); the muted ENSO teleconnection and the sea-ice explanations are hypotheses only; the PBO tropical warm response is a regularity seen in one core plus two Lea data points, and its mechanism is declared beyond scope (§5.8 ¶4); the reinterpretation of Lea et al. as seasonal bias is best_explanation, supported by an amplitude calculation (S then C). The record is a single core and a single transition, so no generalization was tested. The greyscale threshold was chosen to maximize the seasonal difference, which may inflate the estimate; Extended Data Fig. 8 partly addresses this. Composition coded trace_series by inference: conditions were found and the claim rests on comparisons with independent traces, but the headline status is an estimate, not a best explanation. The ordering of analysis steps is inferred from text order, not from a stated workflow. No code availability statement appears in the text supplied.
